newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T sounds conciliatory tone in legal war.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T sounds conciliatory tone in legal war.

text.p: British tobacco-to-insurance group B.A.T Industries sounded a conciliatory tone in its escalating war against American lawyers on Wednesday.

"Yes the rise in legal costs are prohibitive and they take up a lot of time and effort and I don't think its constructive for America or the industry to be permanently at war," said chief executive Martin Broughton in an interview.

B.A.T's American subsidiary Brown & Williamson is facing a string of lawsuits, including 24 so-called Medicaid cases brought by individual states to recover funds spent on treating patients with tobacco related illnesses.

Although B.A.T remains confident of winning the cases -- the industry has never had damages upheld at the end of the appeal process in over 500 cases filed since 1954 -- Broughton sounded a more cautious note.
"We are comfortable that on the law we will win these cases, even if we lose a few on route...it does not set a precedent."
On Friday a federal judge in North Carolina ruled that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration can regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes.

The ruling found that cigarettes could be regulated as drug delivery devices under U.S. federal law, something the tobacco industry has fiercely opposed and cigarette makers could be placed under the FDA's jurisdiction.
"It was very encouraging to win half of it and disappointing to lose the other half. It leads us down the route of prospectively another five years in the courts on this particualr issue.
"And I don't see this as in our interests or America's for us to be forever at war. I think there must be easier ways than for us to spend five years going through the courts.
He said there was little separating the two sides in the dispute and it ought to be possible to settle the issue out of court.

B.A.T's shares, which stood four pence lower at 518p in late trade, are held back by worries over the outcome of U.S. litigation and the prospect of an industry wide settlement of future claims under the auspices of Congress.

Broughton declined to comment on hopes in the investment community of a possible $300 billion settlement of the lawsuits or to talk about the type or extent of insurance cover the company may be able to rely on if it loses a court case.

He was speaking after the group released flat first quarter pre-tax profits of 591 million pounds ($962.3 million), hit by a 22 million pound provision for factory closure and exchange rate movements.
The company repeated a warning made at last week's annual shareholders meeting that if the strength of the British currency persisted it may hold back the group's full-year results.

Total trading profit from B.A.T's financial services business rose three percent to 266 million pounds, with the general business slightly ahead at 142 million pounds and the life companies showing a six percent rise to 124 million pounds.

In North America, insurer Farmers made an encouraging start to the year with all round business growth fuelling a six percent rise in profits to 163 million pounds. But market conditions remained difficult for B.A.T's British business where profits fell two million pounds to 77 million pounds.
While the company expects further rises in premiums in the coming year, it anticipates increases to be limited.

Total tobacco profit of 363 million pounds would have risen by eight percent but for a 22 million pound provision for the future closure of a German cigarette factory in Berlin, which reduced the increase to two percent.
Total group cigarette volumes rose slightly to 167 billion pounds, with good gains in Asia Pacific, Middle East and Africa and Europe more than compensating for reduced sales in North America.

Tobacco profit from the America-Pacific region was lower at 140 million pounds in the first quarter. Reduced sales in a very competitive U.S. domestic market and the loss of contribution from the sale of brands disposed of at the end of 1996 as required by U.S. competition authorities, more than offset the benefit of last year's price increase.
B.A.T's American subsidiary Brown & Williamson saw lower shipments and its market share fell to 16.3 percent from 17.5 percent, mainly due to the sale of the brands. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
